units.translation: But that wretched man, unwept, goes.
We will go and help bury him.
But I will go and try.
I will go to the roof of the house.
But I will go and wail in the house.
But I will go and obey your words.
For from a harsh wind comes a storm.
Unless someone goes to the ship.
You will go.
The black-robed Erinys will not go to the house.
Go, come,
But go to the house.
Go, wretched woman.
Let it go with a fair wind.
Let tears go. Let lamentation go.
Let what is not vain go from prudent faces.
Go, go, all of you, here
O children of the Greeks, go.
Go, falling to ruin.
Go to the holy light of these escorts.
Come here.
Go, indeed, lords of the city.
Let those chosen by lot go.
I will go and do it.
Go and announce it.
Praise them as they go from the house.
As they go from this house to wear down another race.
You speak terrible things, that those who go should care for their parents.

εἰμί [I am] joined with participles of verbs serves as a periphrasis (which Lesbonax p. 179 calls the Chalcidian figure): about which, with examples from poets and prose writers, it is discussed in the Thesaurus vol. 3 p. 258.

it is said with the genitive to indicate origin, with the preposition added or omitted
It is joined with the dative in the sense of having, and it is said not only of things which one can have and possess, but also of thoughts and plans.
ἔστιν [it is] followed by an infinitive means that something can happen, or that there is opportunity for something, or that it is permitted
with accusative and infinitive
ἔστιν [it is] with a relative pronoun or adverb in the formulas οὐκ ἔστιν ὅστις [there is no one who], οὐκ ἔσθ᾽ ὅπου [there is no place where]
Concerning the forms of this verb, which Veitch has accurately treated on p. 199-202, the following are to be noted.

1. The forms of the present are either orthotone or, except for the second person singular εἰ [you are], enclitic: about which more will be said below. The most common are the first, second, and third person singular, εἰμί [I am] (or with elision εἴμ᾽ [I am]), εῖ [you are], ἐστί [he/she/it is]. The third person not only admits elision, but also apheresis (as ποῦ ᾿στι [where is]) or crasis (as κἀστί [and is] and μοὐστί [to me is] contracted from καὶ ἐστί and μοι ἐστί). Of the dual ἐστόν [they two are] there is one example, Ch. 207 δύ᾽ ἐστὸν τώδε περιγραφὰ ποδοῖν [these are two outlines of feet], but more examples of the plural ἐσμέν [we are], ἐστέ [you are], εἰσί [they are].
2. Of the second person singular imperative ἴσθι [be] there are three examples in Aeschylus, a few of the third person ἔστω [let him/her/it be], two of the plural ἔστε [be], about which see p. 104a.
3. Of the optative εἴην [I would be], εἴης [you would be], εἴη [he/she/it would be], and the third person plural there are several examples.
